How many calls does your plumbing business really miss? A 20-minute check
Most owners guess. Here is how to pull your real missed-call numbers from your phone records in about twenty minutes.

Ask a plumbing owner how many calls they miss and you will usually hear "not many." Then they look at the phone log and are surprised. You cannot fix a leak you have never measured, so start with the real number.

## What you need

- Your phone carrier or phone system call log for the last 30 days
- A spreadsheet, or pen and paper
- Twenty minutes

Most carriers and business phone systems let you download or view a call history from your online account. If you use a cell phone for the business, your phone's recent calls list works for a rough count.

## Step by step

1. **Pull 30 days of incoming calls.** Ignore outgoing calls.
2. **Mark the unanswered ones.** These are calls with no connection or a very short duration.
3. **Remove the noise.** Take out numbers you recognize as spam, vendors, or wrong numbers.
4. **Note the time of each missed call.** Pay attention to early mornings, evenings, weekends, and lunchtime.
5. **Check for repeat callers.** Someone who called twice in ten minutes was probably serious.
6. **Count how many you called back, and how fast.** Be honest here.

## What to look for

Add up the total and divide by four to get a weekly figure. Then ask:

- **Are most misses during working hours?** That points to being too busy to answer, which text-back and call answering solve.
- **Are most misses after hours?** That points to after-hours coverage, where emergency plumbing calls often come in.
- **How many were never called back?** These are leads you paid to attract and then lost.

## Turn it into dollars

Take the weekly number of real missed customer calls, multiply by roughly four for a month, then by the share of callers who would normally book, then by your average job value. [Our calculator does this for you](/#calculator), and you can change the assumptions to be as cautious as you like.

If the number is small, you may not need any automation yet, and we will tell you so. If it is large, [we can review the same log with you and show where the gaps are](/contact).

After-hours answering for roofers: what to set up before the next storm
Storms bring a flood of calls at once, often at night. Here is how roofing companies can answer all of them and book inspections.

A hailstorm or high wind can send a whole town looking for a roofer on the same evening. Calls arrive at night and all at once, and the first company to respond usually gets the inspection. The ones that go to voicemail do not get a second chance.

## Why storm weeks are hard on small crews

- Homeowners call several companies and pick whoever answers first.
- Your office, if you have one, is closed when most calls come in.
- Even a full-time office manager cannot answer fifty calls in an hour.
- Messages left overnight pile up, and by morning the best leads have booked someone else.

## What to have ready before the storm

**1. A clear after-hours message.** If a call goes unanswered, a text should follow within seconds that says who you are and asks for the address and a short description of the damage.

**2. A short list of questions.** Keep it to what you need to schedule an inspection: address, whether there is active water coming in, and whether they have already filed an insurance claim.

**3. Rules for true emergencies.** Water coming through the ceiling or a tree on the roof needs a faster response than a few missing shingles. Decide who gets paged and what a temporary tarp visit looks like.

**4. Open inspection slots.** Block out time on your calendar so bookings can land on real days instead of "someone will call you."

**5. A follow-up plan for quotes.** After the inspection, estimates on larger jobs often sit for weeks. A few polite check-ins keep you in the running without pestering anyone.

## A word on honesty

Do not promise what you cannot do. If your crew is booked out two weeks after a storm, say so and offer the first available inspection. Customers forgive a wait much more easily than a missed promise.

## Where to start

You do not need all of this at once. The biggest win is making sure no call goes unanswered, then booking the inspection quickly. Missed call text back for HVAC companies: how it works and what to say
A missed call text back replies to unanswered calls in seconds. Here is how it works for HVAC, what to write, and the mistakes to avoid.

When your phone rings and every tech is on a job, the caller does not leave a voicemail and wait. They search again and call the next company. A missed call text back fixes that by sending a text to the caller within seconds, from your business number, so the conversation starts before they move on.

## How it works

1. Someone calls your business number and nobody picks up.
2. Within a few seconds, the caller receives a text message from that same number.
3. They reply, and the system asks a few short questions: what is wrong, what is the address, and when do they need someone.
4. You get a summary on your phone, or the job is booked straight into your calendar.

The caller never has to call back, and you never have to hunt through voicemails at the end of the day.

## What the first text should say

Keep it short, name your company, and ask one easy question. HVAC has an obvious one: is the system not cooling or heating, or is it something else?

> Sorry we missed your call, this is [Company]. Is your system not cooling or heating, or is it something else? We can get you on the schedule.

A few rules that work for any trade:

- **Say who you are.** People ignore texts from numbers they do not recognize.
- **Ask one question.** A long message with three questions gets fewer replies than a short one with one.
- **Sound like a person.** Skip phrases like "Your inquiry is important to us."
- **Offer a next step.** Booking a visit beats "we will call you back."

## Handle emergencies differently

A no-heat call in January is not the same as a spring tune-up. Decide ahead of time which words mean "urgent" (no heat, no cooling in extreme weather, gas smell, water leaking from the unit) and have those messages page your on-call tech right away. Routine requests can wait for the next open slot.

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Texting people who did not call you.** Only reply to inbound callers who contacted you first.
- **Ignoring opt-outs.** If someone replies STOP, the system must stop messaging them. This is a legal requirement, not just good manners.
- **Setting it and forgetting it.** Read a few real conversations each month and adjust the wording.
- **No person behind it.** A customer should always be able to reach a human when they want one.
